notes.meaning: God gave this message directly to the prophet Joel, whose name means 'the Lord is God.' Nothing else is known about Joel or his father Pethuel. The prophet did not invent these words, but spoke as God's chosen messenger.

Joel calls on the community leaders and all the people of Judah to pay close attention. He asks whether anyone, even in the days of their ancestors, had ever seen a disaster this terrible. The people were to pass the story down through every generation so their children would remember God's warnings.

A massive plague of locusts invaded the land in wave after wave. Whatever one swarm left behind, the next swarm devoured until not a green leaf remained. The four names describe either different life stages of the insect or repeated swarms that stripped the fields bare.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older tradition read the four types of locusts as four foreign world empires that attacked God's people, though many Catholic interpreters understand them as literal insects.

notes.meaning: Joel tells the wine drinkers and drunkards to wake up from their sleep and weep aloud. The swarms of locusts had eaten the grapes right off the vines, cutting off the supply of sweet, fresh wine. Losing the pleasure they lived for was a wake-up call to face God's judgment.

The endless swarm of locusts is described like a powerful, invading army marching into the land. Their jaws could chew through leaves and bark as easily as a lion tears through prey. The Lord calls the country 'My land,' showing that it still belonged to Him even while He corrected His people.

The locusts completely destroyed the grapevines and fig trees, which were essential fruit crops in Israel. After eating all the leaves, the hungry insects gnawed the bark off every trunk and limb. This left the bare wood looking white and dead, ruining future harvests for years to come.

The people of the land are urged to mourn like a young bride whose bridegroom dies before their marriage truly begins. Instead of wearing joyful wedding clothes, she wraps herself in rough sackcloth out of bitter sorrow. God wanted His people to feel genuine, deep grief over their spiritual condition.

The daily offerings of grain and wine at the temple in Jerusalem were forced to stop because the harvest had failed. The priests were in deep mourning because they had nothing to present before the Lord. This disruption showed that regular worship and fellowship between God and His people was broken.

The open countryside was ruined, and the land itself seemed to weep in mourning. The three main staple crops of Israel—grain, new wine, and olive oil—were completely wiped out. Without these necessities, daily food disappeared and temple worship ground to a halt.

Farmers and vineyard workers are told to be ashamed and cry out over their lost harvests. All their hard work in plowing, planting, and tending the wheat and barley produced nothing. Their hopes for feeding their families and selling crops were completely shattered.

Every kind of fruit tree withered away, including grapevines, fig trees, pomegranates, date palms, and apples. Because these harvest seasons were normally times of great celebration, all human joy vanished along with the trees. The loss of the crops left the people feeling empty and hopeless.

Joel commands the priests who serve at the altar to wear rough sackcloth and weep through the night. Since the daily grain and wine offerings could no longer be brought to God's house, the priests had to lead the way in humbling themselves. Merely feeling sad was not enough; they had to turn back to God with sincere repentance.

The leaders are told to call a sacred fast, setting aside food and daily work to focus completely on God. The community elders and all the people were to assemble together at the temple in Jerusalem. There they were to unite their voices and cry out to the Lord for mercy.

Joel cries out in terror because the 'Day of the Lord' is approaching like sudden ruin sent by the Almighty. In the prophets, this phrase refers to special times when God intervenes in power to judge wickedness. The locust plague was an alarming foretaste of an even greater judgment that lay ahead.

differ.view: Many dispensationalists view the Day of the Lord primarily as the future Great Tribulation and the return of Jesus Christ to judge the earth at the end of the age.
Other believers teach that this day referred first to God's near historical judgment on Judah through foreign invaders, while also foreshadowing the final judgment at the end of history.

notes.meaning: The people could see with their own eyes that all food had vanished from the land. With no harvests to bring as offerings to the temple, all religious joy and celebration disappeared from God's house. What should have been festive seasons of thanksgiving turned into times of grief and famine.

A severe drought made the famine even worse, drying out the soil so badly that newly planted seeds shriveled under the clods of dirt. The granaries and storehouses stood empty and fell into ruin because there was no grain to put inside them. The hope of any future harvest was completely lost.

The domestic animals groaned and cried out in deep distress because all the pastures were gone. Herds of cattle wandered aimlessly in search of food and water, finding only bare ground. Even flocks of sheep, which can normally survive on dry and meager grass, suffered from the extreme famine.

Seeing the widespread devastation and the silence of the people, the prophet cries out directly to the Lord in prayer. Intense drought and heat had swept through like fire, scorching the pastures and drying out every tree. When all earthly help fails, crying out to God is the only hope left.

Even the wild animals look up toward heaven, panting for moisture because the riverbeds and streams have run dry. Intense heat and drought had parched the wilderness pastures until nothing remained. The desperate thirst of these beasts served as an unspoken rebuke to the people, who were slow to seek the Lord.
